name: Amina Juma
oneLiner: Builds clinic records that keep working when the power does not.
photoAlt: Portrait of Amina Juma, a woman with short dark hair and glasses, wearing an olive shirt against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Kadi ya Kliniki
work.summary: An offline-first visit card for small dispensaries. Nurses write the visit on a shared tablet. The record waits, then syncs when the line comes back.
work.outcome: Three Ubungo dispensaries stopped rewriting the same antenatal notes by hand after a half-day outage.

work.title: Pause & Send
work.summary: A small queue, written in Swahili, that shows which notes are still in the building and which have reached the district file.
work.outcome: Night-shift nurses can see what has not left the clinic, instead of guessing in the morning.

work.title: Saturday bench
work.summary: A monthly table with nursing students. They take one paper register apart and rebuild a single screen of it, field by field.
work.outcome: A growing circle of nurses who can specify software, rather than only receive it.

journey: I did not set out to make health software. I set out to stop watching my aunt tell her story twice.

She kept a blue exercise book for the clinic and another for the hospital. When the power failed, the afternoon queue started again from memory. I was the niece with a laptop. The first version was ugly. It also stayed open when the bulbs went dark.

What I owe this city is a record that respects the person who already did the careful work: the nurse, the mother, the clerk with the carbon paper. If a tool cannot survive a Tuesday blackout in Ubungo, it is not ready for Dar es Salaam.
whyItMatters: Tanzania’s clinics already hold the knowledge. Too much of it lives in books that cannot travel with a patient from a dispensary to a regional hospital.
When a note survives the outage and the referral, a mother does not begin again, and a nurse keeps the hour she needed for care. That is quiet infrastructure, and it belongs where people can see it.

name: Halima Said
oneLiner: Trains midwives to teach one another, ward by ward.
photoAlt: Portrait of Halima Said, a woman wearing a patterned green headscarf, photographed against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Circle of Hands
work.summary: A ward circle where midwives rehearse difficult moments with one another, in Swahili, after the shift has ended.
work.outcome: Two hospital wards kept the circle after Halima stopped attending. That was the aim.

work.title: Birth-prep cards
work.summary: Illustrated cards for antenatal conversations: what to bring, who may stay, and what a danger sign looks like.
work.outcome: Dispensaries that had set long leaflets aside now use the cards in the visit itself.

work.title: Night-shift notes
work.summary: A debrief page with three questions, short enough to finish before dawn.
work.outcome: Supervisors can see patterns across a month without asking exhausted staff to write an essay.

journey: I became a midwife because my sister’s labour frightened everyone in the room, including the people who knew what to do. The knowledge was there. It did not move.

So I stopped collecting it in my own notebook and started leaving it in the ward. The circle is deliberately small. A midwife will say the true thing to a colleague she trusts before she will say it to a trainer with a flip chart.
I want the next person through the door to meet a team that has already practised being calm.
whyItMatters: Respectful maternity care depends on the people who are actually in the room at two in the morning. When those midwives can teach one another, the standard stays after a trainer has gone home.
Mothers in Tanga then meet a ward that has rehearsed the hard hour, and a new midwife inherits a practice instead of a speech.

name: Neema Shirima
oneLiner: Weaves market cloth that keeps the names of the women who held the stalls.
photoAlt: Portrait of Neema Shirima, a woman wearing an indigo headwrap with a rust band and small earrings, against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Soko Thread
work.summary: Cotton panels dyed with plants from around Arusha. Each panel is named for a market woman who agreed to be remembered, in the form she chose.
work.outcome: The panels were shown in a borrowed school hall, then returned to the families who lent the stories.

work.title: Dye garden
work.summary: A plot behind a secondary school where students grow indigo and marigold for the art room.
work.outcome: Colour for class no longer depends on a single shop in town having stock.

work.title: Pattern book
work.summary: Drawings of cloth structures with the maker’s words beside the sketch, in her phrasing.
work.outcome: Two schools use the book as a starting point for students’ own pages.

journey: I grew up under a table of kanga, handing change up to my grandmother. People speak about cloth as if it were finished heritage. She spoke about it as Tuesday: who had not been paid, whose child needed fees, which colour sold after the rain.
When I began to weave those days into panels, I asked first. Some women wanted their names in the border. Some wanted only the pattern. The work is theirs before it is mine.
A room that cannot say those names clearly is only decorating itself.
whyItMatters: Young people in Arusha are often handed culture as something that happens on a stage they will visit later. Neema’s studio turns that around. The market is the archive, and the school is the workshop.
Students learn that cloth is made by people they can name, and that making it can be a livelihood as well as a memory.

name: Josephat Mushi
oneLiner: Turns roadside repair benches into paid apprenticeships for school leavers.
photoAlt: Portrait of Josephat Mushi, a man with a short beard in a dark work shirt, photographed against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Fundi Path
work.summary: A twelve-month bench in mechanics, welding, and tailoring. A wage starts in the third month, written down at the beginning.
work.outcome: Most apprentices leave with a named employer, as well as the hours they have already worked.

work.title: Open Saturday
work.summary: The yard opens to neighbours who bring a bicycle, a pump, or a school uniform that needs a seam. Apprentices teach the repair.
work.outcome: Josephat can tell who is ready by watching them explain a bolt to a neighbour.

work.title: Employer ledger
work.summary: A shared sheet of workshops in Kilimanjaro that will take a second-year apprentice, with the trade and the town written plainly.
work.outcome: Families can see where the path goes before a young person leaves school.

journey: I sat Form Four, and then I sat on an oil tin until someone let me hold a spanner. The able hands around this town were never the mystery. The mystery was the month between leaving school and being trusted with paid work.
So the yard pays early. Not a fortune. Enough that a parent can say yes. The standard stays high, because a loose bolt is not a kindness.
The page I care about is the one for the apprentice who now runs the Saturday bench and corrects my welds.
whyItMatters: Each year, young people in Kilimanjaro finish school able to learn a trade and short of a place that will pay them while they learn it.
A local apprenticeship with a wage attached keeps that skill in the town, fills workshops that are already busy, and gives a family a path they can visit on a Saturday.

name: Zawadi Kimaro
oneLiner: Sends plain-language sea conditions to small fishing crews before dawn.
photoAlt: Portrait of Zawadi Kimaro, a woman with braided hair wearing a light blue shirt, against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Bahari Ping
work.summary: A short Swahili message before first light: wind, swell, and a plain line about whether night boats should wait.
work.outcome: Two cooperatives on Unguja pin the message at the landing site for crews who share one phone.

work.title: Radio minute
work.summary: The same note, read once on a local morning slot, for boats that never open a handset.
work.outcome: Crews who stepped away from SMS still hear the condition before they cast off.

work.title: Landing-site charge
work.summary: A shared charging box so the cooperative phone is alive at four in the morning.
work.outcome: The message fails less often for the least expensive reason: a dark battery.

journey: I learned the creek by being told to come back if the water looked wrong. That sentence saved people. It also depended on who was awake to say it.
I studied the sea, then I learned to send a sentence a crew can read without a manual. The models are not the product. The product is a person on a wooden boat who changes their mind in time.
If the note is clever and late, it is a hobby. If it is plain and before dawn, it is care.
whyItMatters: Small fishing crews around Zanzibar carry a great deal of the islands’ food and income, and they carry the risk that comes with a changing sea.

A forecast written for a smartphone they do not own does not reach them. A short message, a radio minute, and a charged phone at the landing site do. More boats stay with weather they would have refused if someone had said it clearly.

name: Baraka Mwenda
oneLiner: Maps lakeshore water so families know when to boil, treat, or wait.
photoAlt: Portrait of Baraka Mwenda, a man with a short beard in a khaki collared shirt, against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Ziwa Watch
work.summary: A shoreline sampling round with fishing cooperatives, taken at the same landing sites each month.
work.outcome: A wall chart in two wards shows the weeks when the water needs boiling, in place of a rumour.

work.title: School kit
work.summary: A basin, a turbidity tube, and a lesson secondary students can run without a laboratory.
work.outcome: Four schools keep their own Monday reading and send it to the ward officer.

work.title: Plain-language brief
work.summary: A one-page Swahili note for dispensaries, with no chart that requires a laptop to understand.
work.outcome: Health officers asked for a second print run before the rains.

journey: My father mended nets. I learned the lake by being sent to fetch water, and by being told, some mornings, to leave it. The instruction was always a person’s memory. I studied so that memory could sit beside a sample.

The work is slow on purpose. A number that arrives once a year from a distant lab does not help a household on a Thursday. A number taken at the landing site, read aloud, and pinned where people already gather can.
I am asking the record to be useful to the people who already live with the water.
whyItMatters: Along Lake Victoria, advice about water is often general, late, or locked in a report. Families decide every day anyway.
Sampling at the landing, written in the language of the ward, lets a community act on its own shoreline. That protects children, and it treats fishers as partners in the evidence.

name: Eliud Komba
oneLiner: Keeps a weekly hour for poems, songs, and town news in the languages people speak.
photoAlt: Portrait of Eliud Komba, a man with a mustache and headphones around his neck, wearing a brown jacket against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Sauti ya Jioni
work.summary: A Thursday evening hour: one poem, one song, and one piece of town news, read slowly enough to be repeated at home.
work.outcome: Listeners send lines by hand and by phone. The hour has kept its month for three years.

work.title: Writing circle
work.summary: Twelve young people, a borrowed classroom, and a first draft allowed in any language spoken at the table.
work.outcome: Several contributors now read their own work on the hour.

work.title: Transcript shelf
work.summary: Paper copies of episodes, kept at a community library for the weeks the signal fails.
work.outcome: Students use the shelf when a teacher asks for a local text and the textbook has none.

journey: I was a bus conductor who started reading other people’s letters on the night bus, because the road was long and the jokes had run out. Someone said I should sit near a microphone. I did not know that was a profession. I knew it was a responsibility.
Mbeya does not need me to sound like a capital. It needs an hour in which a grandmother hears a language she trusts, and a student hears that their town is worth a poem.
I keep the tapes. I also keep the spellings the way the writers sent them.
whyItMatters: A region remembers itself out loud. When local poems and news have a regular hour — and a paper copy for the weeks the tower is down — young people can see that serious language is already being made where they live.
The stories stay in Mbeya, and a school gains a text that did not have to arrive from somewhere else.

name: Rehema Lyimo
oneLiner: Plants school gardens that feed the lunch pot and the science lesson.
photoAlt: Portrait of Rehema Lyimo, a woman with her hair in a bun, wearing a straw hat and a green shirt, against a warm cream backdrop.

work.title: Shamba la Shule
work.summary: Garden beds on three school grounds, sized so a class can weed them inside one period.
work.outcome: The lunch pot uses what the beds grow in season, and the surplus is written on the cooks’ list to go home.

work.title: Watering rota
work.summary: A parent and pupil rota that continues through the holidays, posted on the kitchen door.
work.outcome: Two gardens lasted a long dry term, including the weeks after the children had gone home in December.

work.title: Cook’s notes
work.summary: A short page for school cooks on how to use the week’s harvest, written with them.
work.outcome: Less food was thrown away, because the lesson and the meal were planned as one thing.

journey: I was tired of posters about vegetables the children had never held. We have sun. We have a term calendar. We were missing a bed of soil, and a person willing to be responsible for it on the Friday before exams.
The garden is not a decoration for Visitors’ Day. If it does not reach the pot, I have taught a picture. The children know the difference. So do the cooks.
This page is still with the editors, who are confirming dates with the schools.
whyItMatters: School meals and school science are often planned apart. A garden on the grounds joins them: pupils learn to keep a living plot through a dry term, and the lunch pot has food the school grew.
In Dodoma, that is a practical answer to a hungry lesson and a hungry noon.
